result: CRC organoids can be derived from almost all CRC patients and capture the genetic diversity of the disease through establishment of a genetically diverse biobank.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C13 are supported by citation to van de Wetering et al., 2015, which established the biobank used in this study. While the current manuscript does not independently demonstrate this capability, it relies on and validates this prior work.

result: Mutant RAS status strongly correlates with resistance to EGFR-targeted therapies across a panel of patient-derived CRC organoids, with RAS WT organoids showing higher sensitivity to EGFR inhibition than RAS mutant organoids.
evaluation: Claims C3, C16, C17, C20, C35, C43, C45, C46, C47, and C48 are well-supported by dose-response data across multiple organoid lines (Figures 1, 3, 6), including CRISPR-engineered isogenic pairs and patient-derived organoids with various RAS pathway mutations (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF).

result: The effect of oncogenic KRAS on drug response is independent of cellular status (normal vs. tumorigenic) and the presence of additional cancer mutations.
evaluation: Claims C4, C40, C41, and C42 are supported by comparison of drug response profiles between normal and tumor organoids with and without KRAS mutations (Figures 4, 5), showing similar resistance patterns regardless of tumorigenic status.

result: Dual inhibition of the EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway induces a G1 cell-cycle arrest rather than cell death in RAS mutant organoids, in contrast to rapid cell death in RAS WT organoids.
evaluation: Claims C5, C21, C22, C37, C52, C53, and C76 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including live-cell imaging (Figures 1, 3, 7), flow cytometry cell cycle analysis (Figure 8A), EdU incorporation (Figure 8B), and quantification of mitotic/apoptotic events (Figure 3D).

result: In vivo xenograft experiments with P26T organoids confirmed growth stabilization (but not regression) upon high-dose pan-HER/MEK combination therapy, validating in vitro organoid drug responses.
evaluation: Claims C6, C23, C24, C25, C26, C27, and C65 are supported by xenograft data (Figure 2) showing dose-dependent effects and validation through secondary organoid cultures from treated tumors, demonstrating concordance between in vitro and in vivo responses.

result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated homologous recombination was used to introduce oncogenic KRAS G12D mutation into P18T organoids, with no observable differences in morphology or growth rates under normal culture conditions.
evaluation: Claims C32, C33, and C34 are supported by genotyping data (Figure 3A) and morphological observations. The methodology is cited to Drost et al., 2015, and the resulting isogenic pair provides a controlled system for studying KRAS effects.

result: MEK inhibition sensitizes RAS mutant tumor cells to EGFR/HER2 inhibition, with synergistic activity observed when combining EGFRi and MEKi or EGFRi and ERKi.
evaluation: Claims C19 and C47 are supported by dose-response data (Figures 1A, 6B) and Bliss score analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), showing synergistic effects in RAS mutant organoids. This confirms prior findings cited to Sun et al., 2014.

result: Therapies targeting MEK and ERK (without EGFR inhibition) were similarly effective in all organoid lines regardless of RAS pathway mutational status, while therapies targeting EGFR-RAS-ERK and PI-3K/AKT cascades were largely ineffective in RAS mutant organoids.
evaluation: Claims C49 and C71 are supported by IC50 data (Figure 6B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing consistent efficacy of MEK/ERK inhibition across RAS WT and mutant organoids, while EGFR-containing combinations and PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitors showed reduced efficacy in RAS mutant backgrounds.

result: Combining EGFRi with either MEK or ERKi results in more consistent inhibitory effects across a panel of CRCs than anti-EGFR monotherapy, reducing patient-to-patient variability.
evaluation: Claim C50 is supported by comparison of IC50 variability in Figure 6B, showing reduced variability in combination therapies compared to monotherapy, thereby improving both individual responses and population-scale success rates.

result: Cancer cells that survived dual EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway inhibition rapidly restored proliferative activity after drug withdrawal, with the vast majority of arrested cells re-entering the cell cycle within 20-24 hours.
evaluation: Claims C51, C54, C55, and C56 are supported by EdU incorporation experiments (Figure 8B, 8C), live-cell imaging (Figure 8D), and quantification of mitotic events showing widespread resumption of proliferation after drug removal, excluding senescence or minor subpopulations.

result: pERK levels in both P18T and P18T-KRASG12D tumor organoids were severely reduced by afatinib/selumetinib treatment despite phenotypic differences in drug response.
evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by Western blot data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing reduced pERK in both organoid lines, indicating that pathway inhibition alone is insufficient to explain differential cell death responses.

result: Robust dual inhibition of the EGFR-RAS-ERK pathway significantly primes RAS mutant cancer cells for apoptosis, enabling low-dose navitoclax to induce cell death with dose-dependent sensitization.
evaluation: Claims C59, C60, C61, C62, and C77 are supported by dose-response data (Figure 9A), microscopy quantification (Figure 9B), full matrix screens (Figure 9D), and recovery assays (Figure 9C) demonstrating that effective pathway inhibition sensitizes to BCL2/BCLXL inhibition.

result: BCLXL (not BCL2) protects against apoptosis upon targeted inhibition of the mutant RAS pathway in CRC organoids, as venetoclax (BCL2-specific) cannot reproduce navitoclax (BCL2/BCLXL) effects.
evaluation: Claims C63 and C64 are supported by differential effects of venetoclax vs navitoclax in full matrix screens (Figure 9D) and cited findings in lung cancer (Corcoran et al., 2013), identifying BCLXL as the relevant anti-apoptotic target.

result: Triple combination therapy with low concentrations of navitoclax (50 mg/kg) proved too toxic for mice in vivo.
evaluation: Claim C78 is stated as an experimental observation, though data are not shown. This represents a limitation for clinical translation of the triple combination approach.

result: P8T and P26T CRCs are microsatellite-stable (MSS), belong to the same molecular subtype (TA/CMS2), but differ in their number of cancer-specific mutations (230 vs 163 respectively).
evaluation: Claims C28, C29, C30, and C31 are supported by citations to van de Wetering et al., 2015 and Guinney et al., 2015, providing molecular characterization context for the organoid lines used.

result: The sensitivity of RAS WT colon cancer to EGFRi may represent the dependency of normal colon stem cells on EGFR signaling activity rather than acquired oncogene-addiction.
evaluation: Claim C67 is speculative, inferred from similar drug responses in normal and tumor organoids (supported by data) and cited to Wong et al., 2012. While the observation is valid, the mechanistic interpretation remains a hypothesis requiring further validation.

result: Combination treatment of EGFR-MEK-ERK pathway inhibitors may decrease the potency of low-abundant RAS mutant subclones to initiate tumor relapse during therapy against predominantly KRAS WT tumors.
evaluation: Claim C72 is speculative, supported by citation to Misale et al., 2015 but not directly tested in this study. This represents a potential clinical application but requires experimental validation.

result: Drug phenotypes observed in organoids are representative of in vivo responses, and organoid collections will facilitate identification and optimization of effective targeted therapies, warranting testing of novel drugs on organoid panels before clinical trials.
evaluation: Claims C79, C80, and C81 are supported by concordance between in vitro and in vivo data (Figures 1, 2) and comparison with published PDX data (Sun et al., 2014). The recommendations (C80, C81) are reasonable conclusions based on demonstrated capabilities.

result: Background claims establishing the clinical context for RAS-targeted therapies, limitations of current model systems, advantages of organoid technology, and current clinical trial landscape.
evaluation: Claims C7-C12, C68-C70, and C73-C75 are supported by appropriate citations and represent established knowledge in the field, providing context for the study's rationale and significance.

result: Background claims on mechanisms of resistance and toxicity in RAF/MEK/BCL2 inhibition from prior literature.
evaluation: Claims C39, C57, and C58 are supported by appropriate citations providing mechanistic context for the experimental design and interpretation of BCL2/BCLXL inhibition studies.
